titre: Hastings (1066): Harold's Arrow in the Eye, a Disputed Image
accroche: The 1729 and 1730 engravings of the Bayeux Tapestry show a lance in Harold's eye, not an arrow.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the Bayeux Tapestry, one scene shows a warrior raising a hand to his face, a shaft stuck in his eye, just before a horseman beside him is cut down by a sword. The embroidered caption above reads only: “Here King Harold has been killed.” Tradition sees in him Harold II, King of England, who died on October 14, 1066, at the Battle of Hastings, with an arrow in his eye. The problem: the tapestry does not say which of the two figures is Harold, nothing proves it always showed an arrow at that spot, and no written text contemporary with the battle mentions this particular wound.

## What the Earliest Images Actually Show

The Bayeux Tapestry, embroidered shortly after the Norman conquest and generally attributed to a commission by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, Duke William's half-brother, is our most famous image of the scene. But the two oldest known reproductions of this part of the work, the engravings by Antoine Benoît in 1729 and Bernard de Montfaucon in 1730, show a lance at that spot, without the feathers of an arrow. Needle holes in the linen suggest that something was removed or shortened, and feathers added to form an arrow. Historian David Bernstein, in Anglo-Norman Studies, asks why the artist depicted Harold blinded by an arrow when no contemporary written account mentions that detail, and he points out that the work has been extensively restored, with no critical edition that would always let us tell a restored area from an original one. So he does not settle the matter for us: the image remains disputed.

## Silent Texts, Then an Arrow That Arrives in Stages

On the side of the chronicles, the timeline is just as telling. The *Carmen de Hastingae Proelio* (Song of the Battle of Hastings), composed by Guy, Bishop of Amiens, around 1067, a few months after Duke William's coronation, credits Duke William himself with killing Harold, which historians consider unlikely, since such a feat would have been recorded elsewhere. William of Jumièges places the king's death in the morning, during the first fighting, a version judged even less likely. William of Poitiers mentions Harold's death without describing the circumstances. The Chronicle of Battle Abbey, founded on the very site of the clash, goes further: it states that no one knew, in the press of battle, who had struck the fatal blow.

The arrow appears in writing only in the 1080s, in the work of the Italian monk Amatus of Montecassino, whose account is considered unreliable: he also gives Duke William 100,000 soldiers. William of Malmesbury then picks it up, adding that it went through the king's brain and that a knight wounded Harold at the same time, and the chronicler Wace repeats the story in turn. These texts date from several decades after the battle. Modern biographers disagree: Ian Walker thinks Harold probably died from an arrow in the eye, while allowing that a Norman knight may have finished him off, and Peter Rex concludes that it is impossible to say how he died.

## What Can Be Said

The tapestry itself is ambiguous: one warrior holds a shaft stuck in his eye, next to a fighter cut down by a sword, and it is not established which of the two is Harold, or whether both are. As for the arrow, two things sit side by side: a textual tradition that appears in the 1080s and that other chroniclers repeat, and an image whose original state is partly lost to us because of repairs. A confusing battle scene, in which the Battle Abbey chronicle admits that no one knew who had killed the king, has become for many readers a single, sharp image.

repere.texte: The 1729 and 1730 engravings of the scene of Harold's death show a lance, not an arrow; needle holes suggest a modification, and the first text to mention an arrow dates from the 1080s; what the tapestry originally showed remains disputed.
repere.source: Wikipedia, “Bayeux Tapestry” and David Bernstein, “The Blinding of Harold and the Meaning of the Bayeux Tapestry,” Anglo-Norman Studies V, 1983

carte.punch: The 1729 and 1730 engravings of the Bayeux Tapestry show a lance in Harold's eye.
carte.idee: The arrow in Harold's eye is disputed: the 1729 and 1730 engravings show a lance, needle holes suggest a change, and no text before the 1080s mentions an arrow.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The poem by Guy, Bishop of Amiens, composed around 1067: the earliest known account of the battle, written with no mention of an arrow.

quiz.question: Why is the image of an arrow in Harold's eye at the Battle of Hastings uncertain?
choix: Because Duke William had every scene depicting the defeated king's death destroyed
Because no copy of the tapestry predates the battle by less than three centuries
Because no text written before the 1080s mentions an arrow, and the earliest engravings show a lance
Because this scene no longer appears on the tapestry as it is displayed today
quiz.explication: No text written before the 1080s mentions an arrow (Amatus of Montecassino is the first), and the 1729 and 1730 engravings show a lance: the image's original state remains disputed.
